body_markdown:
On a long enough timeline, keeping cars on the road becomes a treadmill, and we spend our time obsessing over tiny bumps in the rotating rubber belt. Sure, there are minute differences in replacing a water pump on a Ford small-block, compared to doing the same job on a[Stellantis Hurricane inline-six](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/inside-the-new-charger-super-bees-600-hp-inline-six-engine/) , but replacing a water pump is replacing a water pump. After all, at the end of the day, a car is nothing more than a self-propelled rolling cart, and how many truly unique and different ways can a person really assemble one of those?


Working on cars doesn’t become a treadmill unless you have a vast amount of experience. I’m not there yet, but I’m trying, and that means tackling new projects and tasks that are not always enjoyable or simple. Growth requires discomfort. However, I never thought a differential would make me squirm, never thought it would teach me a few new lessons.


Getting the new clutches into the carrier for the limited-slip was a process, but it got done.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The pin to retain the spider gears has this hole for a roll pin that needs to be aligned properly.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Red Loctite and proper torque should mean this ring gear never moves.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


That’s a lot of gears in a real small package.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This differential project started because I played with some math before actually undertaking[the LS swap on my 1985 Corvette](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/project-corvette/) . This swap could have been as simple as removing the stock small-block Chevrolet and replacing it with a slightly newer small-block Chevrolet, or as complicated as a thorough reengineering of the car. I’m no engineer, but thanks to a healthy amount of DIY experience and some extensive reading on this particular topic, I felt informed enough to alter more performance variables than just the powerplant—in particular, the transmission and the ratio of the gears in the rear end. Throwing a bunch of power at a chassis is fun. Giving that power what it needs to work efficiently with that chassis can totally transform a car.


When I last touched on this differential project, it was over a month ago. Everything was disassembled and new parts were sitting on the bench. Week after week, I found a litany of excuses to avoid the next step in the project: assembling the clutch packs and measuring shims to establish a baseline gear setup. I kept “discovering” other projects that needed to jump to the top of the list, and each of those projects took until 7:15 p.m., when it was obviously too late to start something else.


Final install of the bearings is a bit of a nervous moment.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


A couple shims hide behind the new carrier bearings.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Gear-marking compound told me how the gears were interacting.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Nothing says “this diff is finally done” like getting out the paint pen.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Just in case it’s not me who next opens up this differential.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The setup of a rear gear is critical to a long-lasting, quiet, and efficient power transfer from driveshaft to wheel hub. The Corvette’s Dana 44 was probably not the example on which to learn: The shims are placed behind the taper bearings, which are press-fit on top, unlike other differential designs that place the shim behind the bearing cone, making it possible to remove or adjust shims without risking damage to the taper bearings. Disassembly sounds tedious, and it can be, but after finally knuckling down and doing it, I can say that it was no more difficult than the camshaft swap in[the LQ4 engine](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/the-real-reason-i-bought-my-project-corvette/comment-page-2/) that now resides under the Corvette’s long, sloping hood.


Sure, there are precise measurements you must get right, but the tools to measure backlash and shim thickness have never been cheaper. Did I have to confirm I was using a micrometer correctly? Yeah, but in my defense, I seem to use it only once a year, and when your safety depends on playing with numbers three places to the right of the decimal point, a refresher course is never a bad idea.


Another good idea? Refusing to let yourself avoid a project. Working with fiddly parts of this differential did not excite me; it only intimidated me. All the parts sat on a bench until I woke up and decided that today was the day. I set up the gears, did the final assembly, and got everything prepared to shove the whole “batwing” back in the car the next morning. Less than 48 hours after I drew a mental line in the sand, I was idling the Corvette about the neighborhood as instructed by the gear manufacturer to help put the final heat treat on the gears.


Upgrading to new Spicer hardware and U-joint straps is a smart move on fourth-gen Corvettes.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The driveshafts got a quick cleanup after the new U-joints.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The “batwing” that mounts the differential to the chassis got Delrin bushings, before getting bolted back into place.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


All ready to go back under the car.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Ready to wrestle it back into place.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Almost time for wheels and tires.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Confronting the next step in the differential project required coming to grips with the fact I would probably not get this diff set up perfectly. First attempts rarely produce perfect results; there is simply too much to learn in the process. I got lucky this time, as all I did was replace the shims on the carrier and pinion with new shims of the same size and then reassemble everything. In this case, you can only check your work once everything is put together, and somehow I was lucky enough that the gear-marking compound bore good news. Sure, reading gear compound is a little like reading tea leaves—you see what you want to see, most times—but the yellow schmoo on the ring gear said the hypoid set was meshing well, with the pinion and ring gear coming together in the center of the teeth with nice wide contact patches. That’s only one metric to determine the viability of the setup, though.


The backlash is the other, and it was not as great. With the factory service manual calling for 5 to 9 thousandths of an inch of movement on the ring gear with the pinion stationary, the best I could do was use a heavy hand and get 4 thou of backlash when I looked at the indicator from the right angle. A little tight. A couple phone calls to friends led me to conclude that I might as well try it. This is a new set of gears, after all, and while the backlash is what allows them to run in together, that running-in will likely produce a little more backlash.


Best practice would be to pull off the carrier bearings and shuffle a few small shims to open up the backlash to book spec. The’s what an engineer would do. We established earlier that I am not an engineer, though, so with a little encouragement from those same friends I have opted to to sacrifice future Kyle’s weekend by running the new gear setup as-is for a bit, and if it becomes noisy or gives any indications of being unhappy, I’ll pull it apart and shuffle shims. Scout’s honor.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I’m barely outside of the “take it easy” period requested by the gear manufacturer, and simply feeling out what the car is capable of has me grinning from ear to ear with each shift. The Corvette accelerates like I wanted it to: It pushes my back into the seat with a force that is going to prove addicting. Time to reconsider my tire budget…


Those who have been keeping up with this project know that there are many more systems on this car I have yet to touch—the suspension and brakes, mainly. That will change, but I think I’m going to (carefully) enjoy the car as it is for a little while as I source the parts and pieces I’ll use to refresh the chassis. After all, winter is just around the corner.
